title: In 12 IBL widefield sessions from 6 mice, cortical activity lags were reliable but did not follow the anatomical hierarchy or pair-specific axonal projection asymmetry
abstract: Question: does the direction of mesoscale activity flow across mouse dorsal cortex follow axonal projections? H1: areas low in the Harris et al. 2019 hierarchy lead. H2: in a pair of areas, the area with the stronger Knox et al. 2019 projection leads, after the mean lag of each area is removed. Data: International Brain Laboratory widefield GCaMP sessions (haemodynamic-corrected, 15 Hz, decision task); 12 confirmatory sessions, 2 per mouse for 6 mice, selected by a fixed rule; 42-48 Allen areas per session. Method: pre-registered plan; lags from the cross-covariance peak with parabolic interpolation at 0.1-2 Hz; mouse-level t-tests, area-label permutations; rule = p < 0.05, same sign in 5 of 6 mice, permutation p < 0.05. Results: lags were reliable (split-half r 0.99 for area lags, 0.97 for pair lags after area lags were removed; mean |lag| 41 ms); dorsal retrosplenial cortex led in all mice. H1 failed: +5.1 ms per SD of hierarchy after position covariates (95% CI -1.7 to 12.0, p = 0.11, 6/6 mice positive, permutation p = 0.62). H2 failed: -4.5 ms per log10 asymmetry (CI -16.8 to 7.7, p = 0.39, 3/6 mice). Without area-lag control, the stronger-projecting area led in 58.7% of pairs (permutation p = 0.006), but this is an area-level effect (net outflow) that spatially smooth surrogate maps reproduce (p = 0.21-0.27). Pair-specific lags repeated within a mouse (median r 0.53) but weakly between mice (0.18). No secondary band, quiescent epoch or global-signal condition met the rule. Limitations: 6 mice from one lab; a planned stimulus-evoked positive control failed because the mice moved fast; midline vessel signals and camera timing can affect lags; Knox and Harris maps come from other mice. Conclusion: widefield lag structure is stable within animals but is not explained by tracer hierarchy or projection direction.
